synopsis: TÜV SÜD frames simulation as a complementary evidence pillar: models must be qualified, and European automated-driving regulation and ISO 34502 require the virtual platform itself to be shown fit for purpose [f1971, f1283, f1717]. It offers independent simulation and model validation, including VIVALDI-style credibility assessment; the cited work is road-regulatory but is presented as relevant to a defensible validation process [f8831, f8832, f16111]. BMW reported on 6 February 2026 that KBA recognized virtual crash tests after a TÜV SÜD audit, but did not specify a percentage reduction in physical testing [f7566, f7857]. TÜV SÜD also supplied physical-test and ground-truth engineering in PEGASUS, illustrating its role in linking simulation to physical evidence [f1583, f16112]. Separately, its September 2024 announcement that it had become the first notified body under Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 establishes that this notified-body route exists, but these facts do not establish acceptance of virtual-only validation for heavy off-road braking [f11214, f15108].

relations.note: Both require demonstrating that the virtual platform is fit for purpose.
Both report the September 2024 first-notified-body announcement.
Both report BMW's February 2026 virtual-crash recognition following a TÜV SÜD audit.
Both identify independent simulation and model validation services.
Specifies physical-test and ground-truth engineering behind the PEGASUS test-lab role.
Qualifies the assessment services' road-regulatory scope and broader validation relevance.
Platform fitness requirements reinforce the need to qualify simulation rather than assume replacement.
Audited recognition without a reduction percentage supports caution about physical-test replacement claims.
Physical testing and ground-truth engineering illustrate simulation's complementary evidence role.
The reported audit provides a concrete example of simulation assessment in regulatory recognition.
